comment: One input, one output. `tests/fixtures/redaction/rules.json` pins the names and the
patterns; this file pins what they do to a string.
The Rust crate crates/sasy-redaction reads it: its tests
run the whole corpus, so a change to the crate that moves any of these
outputs fails its suite. The suite also asserts a minimum size before
comparing, so a merge that emptied this array would fail rather than
leave a green suite pinning nothing.
Every secret-shaped literal here is synthetic. Inputs deliberately stay
clear of the one place a regular-expression engine without backtracking
differs by design: a PEM body past 8000 characters, which a bounded
pattern stops reading and an unbounded one does not. One difference is
not by design and is not pinned here either: a U+FEFF is whitespace to
JavaScript's `\s` and not to Python's or Rust's. The URL run, the URL
userinfo and the parameter value do not use `\s` at all - they carry
the `space_chars` class written out character by character - so what is
left of that difference is the header-name boundary and the
`-u user:pass` flag, where a header line holding a U+FEFF splits into
two tokens under a JavaScript `\s` and stays one token here.
The JWT segments are unbounded: a bound buys nothing, because the
segment class cannot be followed by the `.` that has to come next.
The rows from `def login(password=...` down are the inputs where a
credential shows up in ordinary developer traffic: the .env body, the
JSON, YAML and TOML configs, the Python signature, the shell case arm,
the Makefile line, the curl -H / -u / --password lines, the docker -e
line, the psql and git userinfo URLs, the JSON-encoded quoted URL, the
markdown link, the HTML-escaped URL, the connection string, the
;-separated shell chain, and the header readings.
The rows after those are the shape readings: a word that opens like a
fixed-length key (ASIAPACIFICREGION2026), a branch name and a file name
that open like an OpenAI key, a PEM block that was never closed followed
by prose and a whole key, a pre-signed URL's signature field, and two
lines ended by a bare carriage return.
The rows after those cover the `==`, `===` and
`:=` operators, which the separator must not eat; a reference longer
than fifteen characters; a numeric JSON value, which has to come back
as a quoted marker or the blob stops parsing; a name behind an escaped
quote in double-encoded JSON; an empty userinfo user; a PEM key inside
a JSON-encoded tool argument; the docker-compose and
~/.aws/credentials spellings of an environment-variable name, and a git
diff's removed line; the authorization values that are prose rather than
credentials; a header whose value is quoted and whose name is not; and
Unicode look-alikes for a name, which must not fold onto it.
One row is a limit rather than a reading: a Kubernetes pod `env:`
list, whose name and value stand on two lines of their own, is pinned
byte-for-byte untouched.

The rows after those pin the quoted reader's two rules: a quoted value never crosses a line break, in raw text and one encoding level down, and a quoted value whose content holds no ASCII letter and no digit is not a credential. So a captured `Enter password: ` prompt, a `DB_PASSWORD=` line with an empty value and a shell script that reads a password on a later line all come back byte-for-byte, while a prefixed line - a comment with an apostrophe in it, a file:line prefix, prose - still redacts.

One group is the dotted name. `PARAM_DELIMITER` excludes the `.`, so `spring.datasource.password=`, `db.password=`, `mail.smtp.password=`, `-Dspring.datasource.password=` and `--set postgres.password=` are read by no rule on their own. They are read under a glued `=` and under nothing else: the spaced assignment (`self.password = get_pw()`) and the colon form of a dotted name are pinned untouched here and stated as limits, because the exclusion is what keeps ordinary source unread.

Fifteen rows cover the header name behind an escaped quote. Seven are the header-only names - authorization, proxy-authorization, cookie, set-cookie, x-auth-token, x-goog-api-key, x-subscription-token - in double-encoded JSON: the header name pattern admits the escape between the name and its colon, so a request-headers file written as JSON, and a tool result quoting one back, are both read. The empty value and the single-encoded blob are the controls, and x-api-key is the name the parameter tier already reached. Four are the dotted name reaching the header-word exemption: `gateway.api-key=` and `nginx.x-api-key=` keep a word value, as the bare spellings do. `svc.apikey=not-set` still goes, because `apikey` without the hyphen is not one of the nine header names under any spelling - the bare `apikey: not-set` goes too, so the two readings agree.

Four rows are limits made visible rather than readings. Two pin the backslash that stands in front of a raw line break: it escapes the break in no shell the reader may assume, so the read ends there instead of running on to a closing quote on the next line and deleting a line of a recorded two-line Write. One pins a quoted password written only in non-ASCII letters: the letter-or-digit test is ASCII-only, so a value made solely of non-ASCII letters or of punctuation is kept - widening the test to Unicode would reopen the splice it closes. The last one is the array splice: a JSON array element that ends on a credential name next to a non-string element puts `, 1, ` between the string's own closer and the next quote, that span carries a digit, and the marker goes over it, so valid JSON comes out invalid. It is pinned with what ships and named as an exemption in each suite's JSON invariant; closing it needs a JSON reader rather than a rule about characters. An object is safe, because a quoted key always puts a bare `, ` there.

Two rows are known limits, and each is found by what it holds rather than by where it sits: the HAR headers list - `{"headers": [{"name": "Authorization", "value": "..."}]}` - where the header name is the value of a `name` field rather than the key of its own pair, so no reading here finds it; and the `.netrc` line - `machine api.example.com login deploy password hunter2hunter2` - which separates `password` from its value with a space and nothing else, while every separator form here needs an `=` or a `:`. Both are pinned byte-for-byte untouched.

Five rows are the escaped break in front of a header name, each paired with the raw twin it must agree with: `api-key` and `x-api-key` standing on the second line of a JSON-encoded body, once with a word value that stays (`not-set`, `application/json`, `N/A`, one of them in a numbered Read result) and once with a real key that goes. Three rows are the doubly encoded private key: a Google service-account file, whose `private_key` field already spells its line breaks `\n`, written with the Write tool and read back through a tool result, so each break arrives as two backslashes and an `n` - and the singly encoded field on its own as the control. One row is a query-parameter name that must not fold under Unicode: a query string whose parameter name is spelled with the Kelvin sign (U+212A) in place of its first letter folds onto `key` under Unicode case folding and must not be read as `key`, because the name comparison is ASCII-only; the row is pinned untouched.

Thirty-five rows are the shape crossing. `SHAPE_BOUNDARY` admits the two-character escape as well as a real line break, so a shape is read on any line of a JSON-encoded body and not only the first. Every shape that fires is pinned three ways - once after `\n`, once after `\t` in the numbered form a Read result takes, and once in raw text as the twin they must match: the PEM block, the GitHub, GitLab, npm and Slack tokens, the AWS key id, the OpenAI key, the Google API key and the JWT. With them: a Read of a key file whose numbered lines carry the whole block, a Write whose key starts on the second line after a comment, a file holding two key blocks where both must go, the `-u admin:` flag on a second line with its raw twin, a `postgresql://` userinfo password after an escaped break and after a tab - the one boundary that needs no escape handling, because the letter of the escape is also how a scheme begins - and, as the control, a shape glued to the end of a word (`a\thunterghp_...`), which stays.
